summary:
Nāgāland stands under India's national framework on gender recognition, and no deviation from the national position has been identified for the state at a margin material enough to score separately. A visitor to Nāgāland faces the same recognition, documentation and policing conditions as elsewhere in India.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. The bill removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling, narrows the statutory definition of a transgender person, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. It was approved by both houses and, at the time of the reporting, awaited presidential assent; Human Rights Watch, writing on 26 March 2026, called the amendment a major reversal of the rights established in 2014 and urged the president not to sign it.

The consequences for a trans visitor turn on which category they occupy. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the historically accepted groups fall outside the recognition scheme altogether, and anyone seeking recognition within it must undergo medical certification, which critics describe as an attack on privacy and dignity. The government's stated position is that the narrower definition improves the delivery of welfare schemes; critics warn that it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Care and financial access are set nationally in part and at state level in part. The Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex visitors should note that reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations. The Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Facilities and welfare benefits vary sharply between Indian states, so a visitor's access to trans-specific services depends on where in the country they are. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nāgāland does not appear among the states described as operating such a board in the sources reviewed.

Two official assessments of police conduct point in different directions. A foreign government's December 2025 country policy note describes police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited, more likely in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while interviews with victims documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. Nāgāland's hill districts and its relatively small urban centres would sit closer to the conservative-rural profile that the first assessment identifies as higher risk.

The 2026 amendment is contested on the record itself. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe it as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, and Human Rights Watch calls it a huge setback.
localsOnly:
Residents of Nāgāland who are trans or gender-non-conforming are the people most exposed to the March 2026 amendment, which governs the identity certification they need for domestic documents and welfare access rather than for short-term entry. Those falling outside the historically accepted socio-cultural categories must seek recognition through medical certification, and those outside the scheme entirely have no statutory route to recognition under the amended 2019 law.

State-level welfare boards are the ordinary channel through which Indian residents obtain housing subsidies, pensions and publicly funded surgery, and four other states run such boards. Residents of Nāgāland relying on comparable support would look to state schemes and to national schemes rather than to those other states' boards.

Two national provisions benefit residents directly. The Ayushman Bharat health scheme's April 2024 expansion covers transition-related healthcare for transgender community members, and the August 2024 finance ministry clarification removes any restriction on LGBTQ people opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

The Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines and the conversion-therapy bans arising from them bind authorities in Tamil Nadu and the National Medical Commission nationally; they do not by their terms bind Nāgāland's police or medical councils.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources reviewed contain no Nāgāland-specific material on state welfare schemes for trans people, state police conduct, or any state-level deviation from national recognition rules, so those questions remain unresolved rather than settled either way.

Whether the president has signed the March 2026 amendment, and whether it is therefore in force, was unresolved in the sources reviewed, which describe the bill as approved by both houses and awaiting assent.

No source in the inventory documents trans-specific violence, hate-crime outcomes or court cases arising in Nāgāland itself, and no source addresses Nāgāland's position on the intersex surgery ban that the Madras High Court ordered for Tamil Nadu in 2019.

The extent to which India's 2018 decriminalisation and Article 15 protections are enforced in practice in Nāgāland's rural districts is not sourced; the assessments of police conduct cited here are national or drawn from other states.
